subject: Copywriting
title: Write Like You Talk
description: A quick, practical guide to Write Like You Talk.

hook.text: Gary Halbert wrote his letters as if dictating to a friend. No jargon, no formality—just human talking to human.

buildup.text: Conversational copy lowers resistance. Formal language triggers the 'being sold to' defense.

discovery.text: Read your copy aloud. If it sounds stiff, rewrite it. If you wouldn't say it in conversation, don't write it.

twist.text: Writing like you talk doesn't mean writing poorly. It means clarity, warmth, and rhythm—not grammatical errors.

climax.text: The best sales letters feel like a smart friend explaining why you should try something. That's the target voice.

punchline.text: Read it aloud. If it sounds fake, rewrite. Conversational copy wins.

quiz.question: How can you test if your copy sounds natural?

details.summary: The best sales letters sound like one person talking to another — not a corporation addressing consumers. Short sentences, contractions, sentence fragments, and plain language create a rhythm that feels natural, approachable, and trustworthy.
details.whyItMatters: Conversational writing is not lazy writing — it's strategic. People skim formal copy but read conversational copy because it feels like it was written by a human who cares, not a committee that approved it.
takeaways: Short sentences and paragraphs keep readers moving forward
Contractions and colloquialisms build trust and rapport
Reading copy aloud is the best test of whether it sounds human

faq.question: How do you write like you talk?
faq.answer: Record yourself explaining the product to a friend, then transcribe it. Clean up the rambling but keep the natural rhythm, contractions, and simple words. If you wouldn't say it in conversation, don't write it in copy. Read everything aloud before finalizing.

faq.question: Isn't conversational copy unprofessional?
faq.answer: The opposite. The most successful copywriters in history — Halbert, Schwartz, Sugarman — all wrote conversationally. Formal, corporate copy signals distance and distrust. Conversational copy signals authenticity and accessibility, which are far more persuasive than formality.
